source_text: Ad alia ire festino, sed multum hic rerum admiratione defigor. Qui in alium tantus furor est, ut si Scripturas non intellegis, vel tua dicta non ponderes? Sed ita argumentaris iugiter, ut quidquid ieceris, recurrat in te impetu grandiore. Dixisti nempe, nullam esse causam pudoris, praeter concupiscentiam carnis in genitalibus motibus apparentem.
pass_a_gloss: I hurry to go to other things, but here I am much fixed by wonder at the matters. You who have so great fury against another, that if you do not understand the Scriptures, do you not even weigh your own sayings? But you so continually argue that whatever you have thrown runs back upon you with a greater rush. You have said indeed that there is no cause of modesty besides the desire of the flesh appearing in the genital motions.

lemmas.lexica: LS concupiscentia=eager desire; Blaise Christian usage often sexual desire vs nuptiae

pass_b_english: I hurry toward other matters, yet astonishment at these things holds me fast. What is this great fury against another person, that even if you do not understand Scripture, you fail to weigh your own words? You always argue in such a way that whatever you throw returns upon you with greater force. You said, of course, that there is no cause of modesty except the desire of the flesh displayed in movements of the reproductive organs.

choices.why: Julian distinguishes nuptiae from concupiscentia; do not flatten to 'lust' as a nature-sin substance.
Julian's sacred writings; keep Scripture, not 'Bible' as a later book-name.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
